card.hook: Stand in the middle of the Grand Place and you'll end up doing a slow spin with your mouth open. Gold-trimmed guildhalls rise on every side, so it's hard to take a bad photo here.
card.stand_here: Stand in the middle of the Grand Place, right at the phone icon on the map. Face south first for the Town Hall and its tall spire, then turn to face the King's House across the square.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit a whole façade, or the tower from top to bottom. Use 1x for general views, and try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for carvings high up on the buildings.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the Town Hall tower up with an upright grid line so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually the quietest, and the square is crowded from 10am to 6pm. After dark, switch on night mode and see which lights are on when you get there.
card.selfie_here: Head to Rue des Bouchers, a short walk from the square, and put the Grand Place tower behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a little low so the tower rises over your shoulder. The old houses on Place de l'Albertine, on the walk down from Mont des Arts, are another backdrop with the Town Hall tower in view.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the northeast corner of the square, where you enter from Rue de la Colline, while you stand in front of the guild houses so they can shoot toward the Town Hall spire and the full row of houses.
card.rules_and_safety: Events like the flower carpet or Christmas celebrations can change access to the square, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take four photos, one for each quarter-turn on the spot, and see which direction wins.
card.good_to_know: The paved square measures 68 by 110 metres. Most of it was destroyed in the French bombardment of 1695, but the Town Hall's façade and tower survived, and the houses around it were rebuilt afterwards. The spire is about 96 metres high with Saint Michael on top, and the square has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the middle of the Grand Place, right at the phone icon on the map. Face south first for the Town Hall and its tall spire, then turn to face the King's House across the square.

card.hook: Stand at the foot of the Atomium and look straight up. Giant steel spheres and tubes rush together overhead like the world's boldest game of pick-up sticks.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place de l'Atomium, right at the base of the structure. The Atomium is right beside you, to the west, so turn that way and tilt your phone up.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x on the plaza, because the Atomium is huge and you'll be standing close. Switch to 1x from Boulevard du Centenaire to fit the whole thing in.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, hold the phone low and line up one of the tubes with a grid line so the tubes lead the eye up to the spheres.
card.best_time: The best time depends on the weather and the season, so check the light before you go. The steel spheres catch the sky and change colour as the light changes, and they're lit by LEDs at night, so an evening visit gives you a whole different mood. Try night mode then.
card.selfie_here: Try the reflection pool in front of the Atomium. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold your arm up so the Atomium sits over your shoulder with its reflection in the water below. Or try the southwest corner of the plaza, about 50 m from the Atomium entrance, with the Belgian flag in the foreground. Take a test shot or two, as we haven't confirmed these exact selfie angles.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to walk back down Boulevard du Centenaire, away from the Atomium, so the whole structure fits in the frame with you in the picture.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photography is allowed at the Atomium, but professional or commercial photography is restricted. The plaza and boulevard are free, but going inside is ticketed.
card.challenge: Can you fit all nine spheres into one shot with a person at the bottom, and make them look tiny next to the giant atom?
card.good_to_know: The Atomium is 102 metres tall and was built for the 1958 World's Fair. It was only meant to last six months, but people liked it so much that it stayed. The spheres are 18 metres across, and together they show an iron crystal magnified 165 billion times. They were re-clad in stainless steel in the 2004-2006 renovation.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Place de l'Atomium, right at the base of the structure. The Atomium is right beside you, to the west, so turn that way and tilt your phone up.

card.hook: Everyone walks around that corner in Brussels expecting something huge, then stops dead and says, "That's it?" Yes, that's it, and the surprise is half the fun.
card.stand_here: Head for the corner where Rue de l'Étuve meets Rue du Chêne, then step a few steps away on the Rue de l'Étuve side, off to one side of the crowd. Face the niche at a gentle three-quarter angle, not head-on.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the boy, his niche and some street around him. If people keep wandering into your shot, try 2x from a bit further back. Skip 0.5x here, because it makes the statue look tiny.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the niche on one of the vertical lines and keep the railing at the bottom of the frame.
card.best_time: Early morning is your best bet, when the crowd is thinner. Feast days are busier, so give yourself a bit of patience and take a few shots as people drift through.
card.selfie_here: Squeeze in at the wrought-iron railing right under the niche, on the corner where Rue de l'Étuve meets Rue du Chêne. Step to one side of the crowd instead of pushing into the group in front, use the front camera and try 0.5x so the statue fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pavement at the street junction with their back to the shopfronts, so the niche, the water stream and the basin all fit in the frame, while you pose near the railing.
card.rules_and_safety: You can see the statue from the pavement, but it sits behind railings. Check the official site before you go for any special events or changes.
card.challenge: Can you get the little guy, his niche and a perfectly timed stranger's reaction all in one shot?
card.good_to_know: Manneken Pis is only 55.5 cm tall. The sculpture goes back to a 1619 design by Jérôme Duquesnoy the Elder, and the blue stone niche was added in 1770. The figure on the street today is a 1965 replica, and the original lives in the Brussels City Museum. His wardrobe runs to around a thousand outfits, so no two visits look quite the same.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the corner where Rue de l'Étuve meets Rue du Chêne, then step a few steps away on the Rue de l'Étuve side, off to one side of the crowd. Face the niche at a gentle three-quarter angle, not head-on.

card.hook: Some buildings don't need a clever angle, they just need you to stand back and say "whoa". The King Baudouin Stadium is one of them: a huge curved bowl with room for 50,093 spectators, parked right next to the Atomium.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 60 m south-west of the numbered pin, and face north-east. You're very close to the stadium here, so step back along the open ground until the whole building fits.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the whole stadium in, since it's enormous. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x-5x (depends on your phone) for details like the old gateway or the edges of the stands.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line up the roofline or the base of the stand with a horizontal line so the stadium doesn't look tilted.
card.best_time: A bright overcast day or later in the afternoon gives soft, even light that shows off the structure. Midday sun makes hard shadows and glare on the pale surfaces, and match or event days can fill your frame with crowds.
card.selfie_here: Try Les Lutteurs, the wrestlers statue on the raised blue-stone plinth at the top of the central median of Avenue des Sports. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and put the statue over your shoulder. Check on the spot whether the stadium shows up behind you, because we couldn't confirm that it does.
card.rules_and_safety: The area around the stadium is open to the public, but getting inside depends on events, so check the official site before you go. On busy event days there may be limits on where you can stand.
card.challenge: Get the whole stadium in with a bit of sky above it, then add one person at the bottom of the frame so everyone can see how big it really is.
card.good_to_know: This is Belgium's national stadium and the biggest in the country. It first opened in 1930, designed by Joseph Van Neck, and was rebuilt and reopened on 23 August 1995. Only a renovated gateway near the main entrance survives from the original, so it makes a good second photo. The stadium has hosted European club finals and the opening match of Euro 2000.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 60 m south-west of the numbered pin, and face north-east. You're very close to the stadium here, so step back along the open ground until the whole building fits.

card.hook: Imagine looking down at about 80 European cities laid out like a colourful patchwork, all in one glance. That's the view from up in the Atomium, and it's a fun one.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Atomium, inside one of the upper spheres, at a window that looks back toward the park. From the Atomium, the middle of Mini-Europe is to the south-west, about 3 minutes on foot, so face that way.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x with your phone held close to the glass to fit the whole park in. Then try zoom 2x-5x (depends on your phone) to pick out a few favourite models. Only use zoom 0.5x if the window is big enough that the frame won't show at the edges.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the edge of the park on a lower third line, with the city and sky filling the top so everyone can see how tiny the models are.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or sunset gives the warmest light up on the top-sphere deck.
card.selfie_here: Try the photo spot by the EU turtle, beside the Mini-Europe entrance. Use the front camera, and I can't promise the park is right behind you there, so check the screen before you tap.
card.ask_someone: If you'd like a shot without a Mini-Europe ticket, try the public path outside the park fence, on the far side of the small lake, but check the frame first, because that spot may suit the Atomium better than the park.
card.rules_and_safety: Both Mini-Europe and the Atomium's top-sphere deck are ticketed, and the park closes for winter, so check the official sites for dates before you go. The Atomium area is quite far out of the city centre, so it's probably not the best place to hang around at night.
card.challenge: Find a path or a tree to show the scale, then see how many tiny landmarks you can name in one shot.
card.good_to_know: Mini-Europe opened in 1989 and shows about 80 cities and 350 buildings at 1:25 scale. The Trevi Fountain model was added in 2019 for the park's 30th anniversary. Some models move, including trains, windmills, gondolas and an erupting Mount Vesuvius.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Atomium, inside one of the upper spheres, at a window that looks back toward the park. From the Atomium, the middle of Mini-Europe is to the south-west, about 3 minutes on foot, so face that way.

card.hook: Plot twist: the King's palace in the middle of Brussels isn't where the royal family lives. They're up at Laeken, so you get the grand front all to yourself.
card.stand_here: Head in by the north entrance on Rue Royale and stop at the mid-park bandstand in Parc de Bruxelles. The palace lies to the south, about 120 m from the bandstand, so face south and let the garden's central path lead your eye to it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole long front in one frame. Go to 2x or more for the central porch and balcony. Use 0.5x only if you're close up on Place des Palais and can't fit the building in.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and keep your phone level, because the palace's straight lines show every wobble.
card.best_time: Late afternoon gives the facade its best light. Sundays around the changing of the guard can be busy on Place des Palais, so the park view is calmer.
card.selfie_here: Use the cobbled forecourt on Place des Palais, with the palace behind you. There's room to fit the building in, and early or late light suits it. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tilt it up a bit so the facade sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the bandstand in the middle of the park while you stand on Place des Palais, so they can catch you with the full facade behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks are banned at the palace, and photos are fine without flash. Watch out for crowds at peak tourist times.
card.challenge: Get the central gate dead centre on Place des Palais, then see if a friend can spot a single tilted line in your shot.
card.good_to_know: The palace stands on the old Coudenberg hill, where a medieval palace of the Dukes of Brabant once stood. In the early 19th century, King William I had the old mansions joined up behind a neoclassical facade. The front you see today was built after 1900 on the initiative of Leopold II.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head in by the north entrance on Rue Royale and stop at the mid-park bandstand in Parc de Bruxelles. The palace lies to the south, about 120 m from the bandstand, so face south and let the garden's central path lead your eye to it.

card.hook: Picture a staircase of gardens that works like a giant arrow, with every straight line pointing at a pointy tower in the distance. That's the Mont des Arts, and it's why this is the classic Brussels view.
card.stand_here: Start from Place Royale at the top of the garden or Place de l'Albertine at the bottom, then walk about 1 minute on foot to the west to reach the middle of the gardens. Stand on the upper terrace, on the central axis and slightly back from the railing above the main staircase, and face down the garden towards the lower town.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the gardens, fountain and skyline all in one go. Tap 0.5x if you want the whole staircase and terraces, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pull the Town Hall tower closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the tower on one of the vertical lines and let the fountain and garden paths fill the bottom third.
card.best_time: Go in the hour before sunset or the first hours after sunrise, when the light is warmest and it's quieter. Your photos get a golden glow and fewer strangers in them.
card.selfie_here: Go to the upper terrace at the top of the main steps, right above the main staircase. Use the front camera at 0.5x with your back to the garden, so the Town Hall tower sits beyond it over your shoulder. For a second option, try Place de l'Albertine by the Albert I equestrian statue, where the Town Hall tower sits in the background.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand below the main staircase while you stand on the level above, at the top of the steps, so the stairs make your backdrop.
card.rules_and_safety: Drones are not allowed on the square.
card.challenge: Get the Town Hall tower sitting exactly on a gridline with the fountain below it, then check whether the terraces really do lead the eye straight to it.
card.good_to_know: A first garden opened here in 1910 and was inaugurated by King Albert I. The layout you see today comes from a major rebuild between 1954 and 1969, with a geometric garden by landscape architect René Pechère. The big fountain at the foot of the terraces was restored in 2017, and further work finished in April 2025.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start from Place Royale at the top of the garden or Place de l'Albertine at the bottom, then walk about 1 minute on foot to the west to reach the middle of the gardens. Stand on the upper terrace, on the central axis and slightly back from the railing above the main staircase, and face down the garden towards the lower town.

card.hook: Everyone snaps the Cinquantenaire arch from the avenue, so you'll get a calmer, more graphic picture by doing something sneaky: let the arch frame itself. Shuffle a few steps and watch its openings line up like a stone picture frame.
card.stand_here: Stand in Parc du Cinquantenaire, inside the park on the central axis, and face back toward the arch through its openings. The subject lies to the south-west of this point.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the arch, the colonnade and the lawns all in one shot. Switch to 1x for a cleaner view through the openings, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the sculpture and the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines to keep the columns upright, then tap the arch's stone and slide a little darker so the sky stays blue and the bronze doesn't turn into a dark silhouette.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the light is softer and fewer people are crossing the lawns. Take a few shots as people walk past, then pick the one with the cleanest frame.
card.selfie_here: Head to the lawns along the park's central axis, between the arch and the avenue side, so the arch and its colonnades sit behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and hold the phone a little low so the arch fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the central plaza facing the arch, while you stand on the lawn between them and the arch, so the bronze quadriga and the lawns both fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The park is an open public space, but the museums in the buildings around it have their own entry rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take three steps left, then three steps right, and see which one makes the openings line up in perfect symmetry. Keep that shot and delete the wonky ones.
card.good_to_know: The big U-shaped complex of halls was built for the 1880 National Exhibition, which marked fifty years of Belgian independence. The triple arch was finished in 1905 and inaugurated by Leopold II on 27 September 1905. The architect Gédéon Bordiau began the project, and after his death in 1904 Charles Girault turned the design into the arch you see today, topped by a bronze quadriga called Brabant Raising the National Flag.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Parc du Cinquantenaire, inside the park on the central axis, and face back toward the arch through its openings. The subject lies to the south-west of this point.

The only tripod and selfie rules I saw concern the Arc de Triomphe in Paris and were left out. The top-of-arch terraces (reached via the Royal Military Museum, about 186 steps or an internal elevator, not wheelchair accessible, museum open daily except Monday) are called the 'ultimate selfie spot' by the museum, but from there the arch is underfoot rather than behind you, so I did not list them as a selfie spot; they may suit a separate photo. The Brussels Times article is about 475 days old and the museum's current hours should be checked. The selfie-spot placement is my reading of a photographer's vantage described by the source, not a page stating it as a selfie spot. card.hook: Stand in the middle of this arcade and everything seems to point the same way: two façades facing each other, shopfronts repeating like a drumbeat, and a glass roof pulling your eye down the passage.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Royal Saint-Hubert Galleries, right where the phone icon sits in the middle of the arcade. Face along the passage in either direction, keep to the side so you don't block people, then turn round and shoot the other way.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit in the long view and the glass roof. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then 2x (or higher, depending on your phone) for shopfront details and the motto on the pediment.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the pilasters with the vertical lines so the whole arcade stands up straight.
card.best_time: People walk through at any hour, so take a few shots or a Live Photo and pick the one with the best gaps. If the light is low in the evening, try night mode and steady your elbows against your body.
card.selfie_here: Try the Rue des Bouchers doorway, a few steps in from the street. A 2026 Brussels Tourism guide calls it the most cinematic of the entrances. Or try the Galerie de la Reine entrance on the Grand Place side, which Brussels Tourism's photo guide says gives the most dramatic perspective. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the arcade over your shoulder, and check on the spot which way gives the best background.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the crossing where Rue des Bouchers meets the arcade and look along the gallery, and if they can't fit it all in, have them step back or move to one end.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask a shop's permission before taking lots of photos inside it, especially when it's busy. The area can get crowded, so hold your belongings in front of you.
card.challenge: Shoot the arcade both ways, then hunt down the motto "Omnibus omnia" on the pediment and get a close-up of it.
card.good_to_know: The three glass-roofed arcades, the King's, Queen's and Princes' Galleries, run for roughly 213 metres together. Architect Jean-Pierre Cluysenaar designed them, and they opened on 20 June 1847. They became a historic monument in 1986. The motto means "Everything for everybody".
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Royal Saint-Hubert Galleries, right where the phone icon sits in the middle of the arcade. Face along the passage in either direction, keep to the side so you don't block people, then turn round and shoot the other way.

card.hook: You squeeze down a narrow alley, past restaurant menus and chatty diners, and then you spot her: a bronze girl with short pigtails, only about 50 centimetres tall. Almost everyone says the same thing: "She's so small!"
card.stand_here: Stand at the far end of Impasse de la Fidélité, right in front of the iron grille, where the phone icon on the map is. From Rue des Bouchers the alley leads north, so face north, straight at the bars.
card.zoom: Start at 1x from right in front of the grille. It fits her, her basin and a bit of the alley end. If people crowd the front, try 2x. Use 0.5x only if you want the whole alley, but it stretches the edges.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the statue on your screen so the phone doesn't pick the bars instead, then switch on gridlines and put her in the middle or on a third.
card.best_time: Early morning or late evening, when fewer people are in the alley. The alley is narrow and can be busy, so take a few frames while people pass.
card.selfie_here: The statue sits in a niche at the dead end, so a selfie with her is tricky. Instead, take your selfie in Impasse de la Fidélité near the Delirium Café end, with the front camera and 0.5x if your phone has it, so the lively alley fills in behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The statue is behind a gate in a public alley, and the gate may be shut at certain times, so check when you arrive. One reviewer warns to be careful passing your phone through the gate, because you could drop it.
card.challenge: Get down low, to her level, and snap her so the bars don't hide her face. Bonus points if you catch the trickle of water.
card.good_to_know: Jeanneke Pis was commissioned in 1985 by Denis-Adrien Debouvrie, who owned restaurants in the alley, and she was put in place in 1987. She's the female counterpart to Manneken Pis. People toss coins into her basin, and the coins go to charitable causes. Don't mix her up with Zinneke Pis, the dog statue, which is elsewhere in the city.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the far end of Impasse de la Fidélité, right in front of the iron grille, where the phone icon on the map is. From Rue des Bouchers the alley leads north, so face north, straight at the bars.

selfie_spots.why: Travel pages describe this alley as a hidden, lively setting near Delirium Café, and the surrounding streets are described as offering colourful backdrops, but no page says where to stand with the statue behind you.

card.hook: You'd expect a comics museum to be loud and cartoonish, but this one is a calm, symmetrical stone beauty that used to sell fabric. Horta designed it in 1906, and it looks best in a nice straight-on shot.
card.stand_here: Stand on rue des Sables (Zandstraat) right in front of the Belgian Comic Strip Center and face the façade. Step back as far as the pavement allows so the whole frontage fits.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural look. If you can't step back far enough, try 0.5x, but the edges can stretch. For close-ups of the arches and railings, use 2x or 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the centre of the entrance up with the middle line, and keep your phone level so the tall pilasters stay upright.
card.best_time: Soft, even daylight suits the stone best, so an overcast day is great. Earlier in the day it's often quieter on the pavement.
card.selfie_here: Try the big Tintin mural just outside the museum at Rue des Sables 20. Use the front camera at 0.5x and stand in front of it. Heads up: the museum might not fit in the frame, so check the screen before you snap. Inside, the entrance staircase is a pretty Art Nouveau backdrop, if the museum lets you photograph there.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a museum, so check the official site for entry and photography rules before you go. Ask at the entrance what you may photograph indoors. The façade can be photographed from the street.
card.challenge: Take one shot where every pilaster stands up straight like a ruled line, then one close-up of the wrought ironwork.
card.good_to_know: The building opened in 1906 as the Magasins Waucquez, built for the textile merchant Charles Waucquez. It's the only surviving example of a series of department stores Horta designed. It was protected as a monument in 1975, restored in the late 1980s, and the museum was inaugurated in 1989.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on rue des Sables (Zandstraat) right in front of the Belgian Comic Strip Center and face the façade. Step back as far as the pavement allows so the whole frontage fits.

card.hook: This courthouse is so huge it makes the whole square look like a toy set, and right now it's wearing scaffolding like a slightly awkward scarf. Don't let that put you off, because the steps and columns still look great.
card.stand_here: Start on Place Poelaert, right in front of the main entrance, and face the building so you're looking straight up at the front. Step back as far as the square lets you so the whole width fits in.
card.zoom: Try zoom 0.5x from the square to fit the full front and the steps in. Switch to 1x for a calmer view of the columns and entrance, then go to 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the dome and carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people on the steps. Tighter shots of columns, steps and carvings often look cleaner than the full front, since the scaffolding hides parts of it.
card.selfie_here: Head to the esplanade (terrace) beside the Palace on Place Poelaert and face out over the lower city, so the palace is behind you. Use the front camera, or try 0.5x to squeeze more building in over your shoulder. The main staircase is also a popular place for a photo, and a person on the steps helps show the scale.
card.ask_someone: Over at the Mont des Arts garden on the hilltop, ask a passer-by to take your photo with the palace in view across the city.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography may be restricted in some areas inside the Palace of Justice, so check signs or ask staff. It's a working courthouse, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside. One traveller review says Place Poelaert is a common place for protests and demonstrations.
card.challenge: Get a shot where you look tiny on the big steps, with the columns standing perfectly straight beside you.
card.good_to_know: Joseph Poelaert designed the Palace of Justice, and it went up between 1866 and 1883. It covers about 26,000 square metres and is reputed to be the largest building put up in the 19th century. The dome was destroyed in the Second World War and rebuilt higher than before.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start on Place Poelaert, right in front of the main entrance, and face the building so you're looking straight up at the front. Step back as far as the square lets you so the whole width fits in.

card.hook: Grey sky over Brussels? Don't worry, this facade doesn't care. The carved stone looks great even on a dull day, and the big open square gives you room to step back and fit the whole thing in.
card.stand_here: Stand in the middle of the Parvis Sainte-Gudule, the wide forecourt just east of the Boulevard de l'Impératrice. From there the cathedral lies to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot, so face it and step back until both towers fit.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole twin-towered facade in the frame. Use 0.5x if you're close or want more of the square. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the towers, gargoyles and pinnacles.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the two towers up with the vertical lines so the building doesn't look like it's leaning.
card.best_time: Afternoon or early evening is your best bet, when the sun is likely to fall on the west-facing facade. Want fewer people on the square? Go early in the morning.
card.selfie_here: Climb the front steps of the cathedral and turn so the west facade rises behind you. Use the front camera, and hold it a little low and at arm's length so the towers fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back across the square from the facade while you stand on the steps, so the whole front fits in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Indoor photos are allowed, but no flash inside. Check the official site before you go, as access may be restricted during services or events.
card.challenge: Gargoyle hunt: walk closer, zoom in and find the grumpiest face up on the stonework.
card.good_to_know: Building began in the 11th century, and by the 16th century the cathedral had largely reached the Gothic form you see today. It's about 110 metres long, and the twin towers are more than 60 metres high. It's also Belgium's national church, so it's often used for royal weddings and state ceremonies.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the middle of the Parvis Sainte-Gudule, the wide forecourt just east of the Boulevard de l'Impératrice. From there the cathedral lies to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot, so face it and step back until both towers fit.

card.hook: Behind this calm, perfectly symmetrical front is a whole museum of surrealism. The pale stone and tall windows make a tidy frame, so let the building be the sensible one for once.
card.stand_here: Head to the Place Royale/Koningsplein in Brussels' Royal Quarter and stand at the phone icon on the map, right at the Magritte Museum. Face the front of the building, and step back as far as is safe to fit it all in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the whole front and a bit of the square. Switch to 1x for a natural view, then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for the doorway, windows and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the building's edges up with the vertical lines so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone than midday. Early on a weekday is likely to be quieter on the square, and after dark you can use night mode and hold your phone steady against your body or a wall.
card.selfie_here: Try the upper terrace balustrade of Mont des Arts, directly above the main staircase, looking out over the old town. Use the front camera at 0.5x and the museum should be up the hill behind you, though check your screen as you turn.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by on the square in front of the building, then stand in front of the façade so they can fit you and the whole front in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks and flash are strictly prohibited inside the museum. Photos are allowed for private use, but a few works can't be photographed at the lenders' request, so check the official site for the photo rules before you go in.
card.challenge: Get a shot with a person standing in front of the building for scale, then try a playful angle that Magritte himself might raise an eyebrow at.
card.good_to_know: The building went up after the Palace of Coudenberg burned down in 1731, and it has been a hotel and a jeweller's shop before becoming a museum. The museum opened on 2 June 2009 and shows some 200 works by René Magritte, including The Empire of Light. The façades and porticoes around the square were given heritage protection in 1951.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the Place Royale/Koningsplein in Brussels' Royal Quarter and stand at the phone icon on the map, right at the Magritte Museum. Face the front of the building, and step back as far as is safe to fit it all in.

card.hook: You come up the lawn from Simonis metro and suddenly a huge green copper dome and two towers pop up above the trees. It's hard to miss, and it's very hard to fit in one photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on the sloping lawn in Parc Elisabeth, on the walk up from Simonis metro, and face the basilica. Walk back along the grass until the whole church is in view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole building with the lawn and trees in front. Then try zoom 2x to bring the dome and twin towers closer. If you move to the forecourt, switch to zoom 0.5x, because the building is too big to fit at 1x.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the dome and towers on the upper line with the lawn filling the bottom third, then tap the green dome and slide it a little darker if the sky is bright so the copper keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go in the afternoon if you want the front of the church lit up, because in the morning the facade is in shade.
card.selfie_here: Use the green sloping lawn inside Parc Elisabeth, on the walk up from Simonis metro, and turn your back on the basilica so it rises behind you. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x so you and the big church both fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand well back on the forecourt (Parvis de la Basilique) so the whole church fits, while you stand in front of the facade and its steps.
card.rules_and_safety: The basilica is a place of worship with its own visiting arrangements and a paid dome gallery, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a tree or the curve of a path to frame the church from the side, and make sure the top of the dome isn't cut off.
card.good_to_know: King Leopold II laid the first stone in 1905, but the two world wars interrupted the work and the basilica was only finished in 1970. The dome is 89 metres high and the two towers by the entrance are 65 metres. It is the largest church in Belgium.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the sloping lawn in Parc Elisabeth, on the walk up from Simonis metro, and face the basilica. Walk back along the grass until the whole church is in view.

selfie_spots.name: Parc Elisabeth lawns on the approach to the basilica

card.hook: Picture a tiny glass town tucked into a hilly royal garden, with a palace parked right next to it. That's Laeken, and yes, it's as dreamy as it sounds.
card.stand_here: Stand in Parc Royal de Laeken (the Royal Gardens), on the palace side of the greenhouses. The greenhouses are to the south-east of you, so face that way and look across the gardens at the glass rising beside the palace.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the glasshouses beside the palace. Go 0.5x if you want more lawn in front, then zoom 2x-5x (depends on your phone) to pick out a single dome or roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the glass, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky doesn't wash out the roofs.
card.best_time: Afternoon or evening light is the one to aim for, because the palace façade faces north-west. Just remember the greenhouses open for only about three weeks each spring (roughly late April to May), so check dates first.
card.selfie_here: Try Avenue du Parc Royal, on the stretch just after you leave the main greenhouse building. The palace is in front of you and the glass domes come into view behind you, so use the front camera at 0.5x and let the domes peek over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo in the Royal Gardens spot where the greenhouses sit alongside the palace, with you standing in front of the glass so the whole complex fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the marked path, since only part of the park is open. Photos for personal use are generally fine inside, but commercial shooting usually needs authorisation from the Royal Palace, and drones are typically prohibited around royal residences.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole glass town, then one close-up of a single dome, and see if friends can guess they're the same place.
card.good_to_know: King Leopold II commissioned the greenhouses, and they were built between 1874 and 1905, first to designs by architect Alphonse Balat. The round Winter Garden is the biggest building, about 57 metres across and 25 metres high. Close by, the neoclassical Orangery dates from 1817 to 1819, and its façade with the orange tree outside makes a good second picture.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Parc Royal de Laeken (the Royal Gardens), on the palace side of the greenhouses. The greenhouses are to the south-east of you, so face that way and look across the gardens at the glass rising beside the palace.

card.hook: This church never got its two towers, and that's a gift for your photo. The roofline is lower and more broken than you'd expect, so the gables, turrets and stonework give the picture plenty to look at.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Jardin du Petit Sablon, directly across the road from the Church of Our Lady of Victories. Face west, and the Gothic front is right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole front. If you're too close to fit it all in, drop to 0.5x and keep your phone level so the walls don't lean. Then try 2x for the carved details and statues.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stonework, then slide it darker if the bright sky is washing out the detail, and switch on gridlines to keep the vertical lines straight.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the front of the church is lit rather than in shadow. Early in the day is worth a try for fewer people, but check the light when you get there, because it can change quickly.
card.selfie_here: Head into the Square du Petit Sablon, the park opposite, and stand by the central fountain with the church front across the square. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and let the church sit over your shoulder, or try 0.5x to get more of it in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the park across from the church front, so the whole facade and you both fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the outside from the public street and the park opposite. The inside is a place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and dress expectations.
card.challenge: Zoom to 2x and see how many of the carved statues you can spot. There are 57 of them, so you'll have plenty to find.
card.good_to_know: It's one of the three Gothic churches still standing in the centre of Brussels. Building began around 1400 and took about a century. Much of the carving you see outside was added later, with 57 statues put in place between 1917 and 1937, and the church was listed as a historic monument in 1936.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Jardin du Petit Sablon, directly across the road from the Church of Our Lady of Victories. Face west, and the Gothic front is right in front of you.

card.hook: The Bourse is covered in columns, carvings and sculpture, so you can fill half your camera roll without ever going inside. Your only real problem is deciding where to start.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place de la Bourse, at the foot of the front steps. Face south-east towards the columned facade, and the whole building fits in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the full facade from the square. If crowds or café tables stop you stepping back, switch to zoom 0.5x to get the steps and lions in the foreground. Then try zoom 2x or more (depends on your phone) for the carvings and sculptures.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning before about 10:00, or around golden hour before dusk, when the light is cleaner. Skip midday on summer weekends, when café furniture and crowds fill the square.
card.selfie_here: Sit or stand on the front steps under the columned entrance, where lots of visitors take their photos. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the columns and lion statues fill in behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is open public space, but the building is now a museum, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
card.challenge: Find the pair of lion sculptures beside the main staircase and get both of them in one shot, with you looking suitably unimpressed (or very impressed, your call).
card.good_to_know: The Bourse Palace was built as Brussels' stock exchange and now houses the Belgian Beer World museum. Architect Léon-Pierre Suys built it between 1868 and 1873 on the old Butter Market site on Boulevard Anspach. The young Auguste Rodin may have worked on some of the friezes.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Place de la Bourse, at the foot of the front steps. Face south-east towards the columned facade, and the whole building fits in one frame.
